strengths: The paper proposes an intuitive and potentially useful idea: approximate RHO-style data values by comparing each example's loss with and without relevant holdout demonstrations in context, avoiding a separately fine-tuned reference model.
The empirical scope is broad, covering SFT, DPO, and SimPO; four LLaMA/Qwen backbones; full fine-tuning and LoRA; and both quality- and domain-oriented selection settings.
Results against ordinary unweighted training are consistently positive, and comparisons use the same reweighting framework for the principal scoring baselines.

The paper includes useful implementation details, runtime measurements, prompts, dataset splits, and ablations over demonstration count, score-update frequency, filtering, and embedding model. The presentation is generally clear and visually polished. weaknesses: The central ICA approximation is not convincingly justified or validated. The manuscript moves from a Bayesian RHO-Loss identity to the assertion that conditioning on a few demonstrations approximates training on the holdout set, but provides no theorem, error analysis, or empirical comparison with the actual post-update holdout loss. The abstract's claim of equivalence under local linearization is not derived in the paper.

The evaluation is insufficiently robust for the main claims. Every model is trained only once, so there is no estimate of training variance. Repeated GPT evaluations at temperature zero do not address this issue. There is also no human validation of the judge, task-specific evaluation, or independent benchmark evaluation.

The sole main metric asks GPT-4o which response is closer to a single reference in content, length, and style. This can reward superficial target-style or response-length imitation rather than correctness or general alignment; the paper's own sports example emphasizes this concern. Judge order randomization, position-bias controls, ties, and confidence intervals are not reported.

Important controls and competitive baselines are missing. In particular, there is no embedding-similarity-only baseline, despite kNN retrieval being integral to the method; nor are there current-loss-only, conditional-loss-only, random-weight, length-matching, or gradient/influence baselines. These are necessary to establish that ICA, rather than retrieval or generic reweighting, causes the gains.

The method generally does not outperform RHO-Loss: many reported win rates against RHO-Loss are below 50%, including most preference-optimization settings. Thus the evidence mainly supports a compute/performance tradeoff, while claims of consistent gains or broadly comparable performance need more careful qualification.

Several methodological claims conflict with the actual experiments. The paper describes dynamically changing scores, but its default and all main experiments compute scores only once at initialization. The purportedly adaptive advantage is therefore not demonstrated in the primary results.

The reweighting design is under-justified. Batchwise min-max normalization always assigns one example weight zero and another weight one, is unstable when score ranges are small, and is undefined when all scores coincide. Equation 9 also omits normalization by batch size or total weight, confounding data valuation with the effective learning rate. Relevant safeguards and controls are absent.

There are technical and reproducibility problems in the exposition. The stated DPO and SimPO equations use probability ratios/probabilities where the standard objectives use log-probabilities, and the exact construction of in-context demonstrations and conditional losses for preference pairs is not specified by the provided query-answer prompt. Code is only promised for future release.

The designated holdout examples are included in the training data in several splits, and the relationship between original and cleaned Alpaca examples may also produce overlapping prompts. Although methods may share this data, calling it a holdout set is misleading and makes the generalization interpretation less clean. Overall, the promising idea is not supported by sufficiently diagnostic theory or evaluation for acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper presents a simple, practically appealing idea: use in-context demonstrations from a target holdout set to score and reweight fine-tuning examples without training an auxiliary reference model.
The empirical study spans SFT, DPO, and SimPO, two model families, multiple model sizes, full-parameter tuning and LoRA, and both quality-focused and domain-focused settings.
The comparisons consistently use the same reweighting framework for ICA, RHO-Loss, and one-shot scores, helping isolate the effect of the scoring rule.
The paper includes useful ablations on demonstration count, score-update frequency, filtering, and embedding choice, as well as a runtime comparison suggesting low overhead.
The presentation is generally organized and provides datasets, prompts, training hyperparameters, and algorithmic pseudocode.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is not established. Equation 6 simply assumes that conditioning on a few demonstrations approximates a model trained on the holdout set. Citing work that interprets some forms of in-context learning as implicit gradient descent does not justify this approximation for instruction-tuned LLMs, arbitrary demonstrations, or preference losses. The abstract additionally claims a local-linearization equivalence to a first-order update, but no corresponding theorem, derivation, assumptions, or experiment appears in the paper.

The paper never directly validates its defining approximation. It should compare ICA scores with actual post-update holdout losses, gradients, influence estimates, or retrained-model scores and report rank correlations and selection precision. Showing that target-domain examples receive higher average scores does not demonstrate that ICA estimates the quantity claimed in Equation 6.

The evaluation is too weak to substantiate broad claims about improved alignment. The only main metric is a forced-choice GPT-4o judgment of which output is closer to a single dataset reference, explicitly considering reference length and style. There is no human validation, judge-bias analysis, tie option, established alignment benchmark, task metric, or absolute quality measurement. The response-length analysis suggests that the method may partly optimize superficial reference style rather than general alignment quality.

Every model is trained only once. Repeating the judge on the same fixed outputs measures evaluator determinism, not training variance, so it does not support the statement that reporting one training run is sufficient. Confidence intervals and variability across training seeds are absent.

Several nominal holdout sets are included in the training data: the Yahoo and SHP-2 constructions explicitly add holdout examples to training, UltraFeedback uses all training examples after selecting its holdout subset, and Alpaca appears to exclude test correspondences but not holdout correspondences. This makes the terminology and optimization setup misleading and raises leakage concerns; genuinely disjoint target-development and test sets are needed.

The default method computes scores only once at initialization and freezes them throughout training. Thus the main experiments do not realize the paper's repeatedly emphasized benefit of dynamically reevaluating data value as parameters evolve. The modest gains from more frequent updates are tested in only one setting.

The baseline coverage is limited for a data-selection paper. There are no gradient-similarity or influence-based methods such as LESS/GraNd-style alternatives, simple loss-based reweighting, embedding-similarity weighting, random weighting/filtering, or strong heuristic quality and domain-selection baselines. Consequently, it is unclear whether ICA is necessary or whether similar gains follow from much simpler signals.

There are serious reporting inconsistencies. Table 6 says results are compared with the default k=3 configuration but nevertheless reports a 48.03% win rate for k=3 against that same default; the main text also discusses k=10 although Table 6 lists only k=1,3,5. The DPO and SimPO preliminaries write objectives using raw sequence probabilities where standard formulations require log-probabilities/log-ratios. These errors reduce confidence in both the exposition and implementation.

The min-max batch normalization is poorly justified and potentially unstable: every batch forces one example to weight zero and another to weight one, is sensitive to outliers, and changes the effective gradient scale without an explicit normalization by the sum of weights. There is no ablation against softmax, rank-based, clipped, or mean-normalized weighting, nor analysis of degenerate batches with nearly equal scores.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the reported hyperparameters: code is only promised for future release, exact generation settings and output-order randomization for evaluation are unclear, and the construction and formatting of preference demonstrations are not sufficiently specified. Overall, the idea is promising but the missing validation of the core approximation and the inadequate evaluation constitute major weaknesses for a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem and proposes a simple, intuitive ICA score that avoids training the auxiliary holdout model required by RHO-Loss.

The empirical study is broad in several useful dimensions: SFT, DPO, and SimPO; two model families and multiple scales; full fine-tuning and LoRA; and both quality- and domain-oriented selection settings.
Results are consistently favorable against ordinary training and One-Shot scoring, while performance is generally competitive with the substantially more expensive RHO-Loss baseline.
The ablations cover several consequential implementation choices, including the number of demonstrations, score-update frequency, filtering versus reweighting, and embedding model.

The method appears practically attractive: implementation is straightforward, the paper supplies training and prompt details, and the reported overhead is much lower than that of the principal baseline.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification is substantially overstated. The crucial approximation that conditioning on holdout demonstrations simulates training on the holdout set is motivated mainly by prior observations about in-context learning; no theorem, error characterization, or direct empirical validation establishes that ICA approximates the post-training holdout loss. The abstract's claimed local-linearization equivalence is not actually developed in the manuscript.

The evaluation is too narrow for the central alignment claims. Performance is measured only by GPT-4o preference for whichever response is closer to a single reference, rather than by established instruction-following benchmarks, human evaluation, task accuracy, or independent quality metrics. This can reward superficial imitation of reference length and style; the Sports example, where the method returns 'Polo.' to a question whose reference is 'A Jockey.', illustrates this concern.

Every model is trained only once. Repeating the deterministic judge evaluation does not quantify variation from optimization, sampling, or data ordering, so the reported differences near 50%—including several comparisons with RHO-Loss and the ablations—lack statistical support.

The main setting computes ICA scores only once before training, despite adaptivity to evolving parameters being presented as a principal advantage. The dynamic version is tested narrowly on one model and dataset, and its small gains are not supported by repeated runs.

The baseline set is limited given the extensive related literature cited. There are no comparisons with strong influence/gradient-based selectors such as LESS or cheaper heuristic controls such as response length, similarity-only weighting, or loss-only weighting. This makes it difficult to isolate whether ICA itself drives the gains.

There is no direct sanity check against the quantity ICA purports to approximate—for example, correlation with actual holdout-loss changes after candidate updates, ranking agreement with an expensive oracle, or sensitivity to holdout corruption and representativeness.

The max-min batch weighting is under-specified and introduces potential confounds: it changes effective gradient scale relative to standard training, has an undefined equal-score case, and forces at least one example in every batch to zero weight. Controls for normalization and effective learning rate are missing.

The reported 1.5% overhead is measured only for one relatively small configuration and omits a sufficiently transparent end-to-end accounting across the larger datasets and model sizes, limiting confidence in the general efficiency claim.

strengths: The proposed ICA score is simple, intuitive, and potentially useful: it avoids training the auxiliary holdout model required by RHO-Loss and can be integrated into SFT, DPO, and SimPO.
The empirical study covers several model families and sizes, full-parameter and LoRA training, multiple alignment objectives, domain targeting, noisy GSM8K data, and relevant baselines.
Results consistently show substantial improvements over unweighted training and one-shot scoring, while generally matching RHO-Loss at lower reported computational overhead.
The appendix includes useful ablations, runtime measurements, absolute metrics, limited multi-seed experiments, prompts, and qualitative examples.
weaknesses: The central in-context approximation is insufficiently validated. Conditioning on a few demonstrations is asserted to approximate training on the holdout set, but the paper provides neither an error analysis nor direct experiments correlating ICA scores with actual post-update holdout loss or retraining-based rankings. Downstream gains alone do not establish the claimed interpretation.

The Bayesian derivation contains a sign error: the candidate-independent current holdout-loss term in Equation 3 should be added when converting the displayed log-probability identity to negative log loss, not subtracted. Although this constant does not change candidate rankings, the stated equality and interpretation as an estimated holdout loss are incorrect.

The main experiments use R=1, so scores are computed only before training and do not evolve with model parameters. This contradicts prominent claims that the method dynamically reevaluates examples as the model evolves; dynamic scoring is tested only in a narrow ablation.

Important experimental details appear inconsistent or incomplete. Alpaca normally contains about 52K examples, making the reported 84,022-example training split impossible under the stated construction, and the reported Yahoo split total does not follow from its described per-domain counts. The preference-data in-context formatting and conditional DPO/SimPO score computation are also not specified by the supplied prompts.

The displayed DPO and SimPO objectives omit log probabilities and therefore are not the standard objectives claimed in the text. Together with the dataset inconsistencies, this raises concerns about whether the manuscript accurately specifies the actual implementation.

Most headline results rely on a single GPT-4o judge and one training run, without human evaluation, confidence intervals, tie handling, or a stated candidate-order randomization protocol. Multi-seed analysis is limited to one SFT dataset, while many comparisons against RHO-Loss are near 50%.

The weighting rule is underspecified and potentially unstable: min-max normalization is undefined when all batch scores coincide, gives zero weight to at least one example, and is difficult to reconcile with the reported per-device batch size of one without explaining cross-device or gradient-accumulation handling.

The paper calls the method principled data selection, but the strongest evidence mainly shows target-style matching under reweighting. Comparisons with LESS and GREATS are narrow and nearly tied, and the GSM8K results do not outperform ordinary SFT on clean data. Overall, the empirical breadth does not resolve the central soundness and reproducibility issues.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: selecting or reweighting fine-tuning data using a small target-quality holdout set while avoiding repeated model training.
The proposed ICA score is simple and potentially useful. Reusing the current model for in-context scoring avoids the separately trained reference model required by RHO-Loss.
The empirical study is broad in surface coverage, spanning SFT, DPO, SimPO, full fine-tuning, LoRA, four model configurations, multiple datasets, and a corrupted GSM8K setting.
Results against ordinary training are consistently favorable, and the GSM8K experiment provides stronger task-based evidence than the reference-similarity evaluations alone.
The appendices include useful implementation details, prompts, dataset splits, runtime measurements, several ablations, and limited multi-seed experiments.
weaknesses: The central approximation is not validated. The paper assumes that conditioning on a few retrieved holdout demonstrations approximates training on the holdout set, but reports no correlation or ranking agreement between ICA scores and the actual change in holdout loss after gradient updates. Consequently, the main claimed interpretation of the score remains speculative.

The theoretical presentation overstates rigor. The Bayesian identity concerns posterior-predictive probabilities, which are not generally equivalent to predictions from an ERM-trained neural network denoted by θ*(D). Equation 3 also appears to have the wrong sign on the candidate-independent holdout-loss term. Although that sign does not change the eventual ranking score, it makes the stated equality incorrect.

The DPO and SimPO equations omit the log probabilities required by their standard objectives, despite π being defined as a probability. Moreover, the claimed extension of ICA to preference losses is relegated to an assertion, and the supplied in-context prompt only explains the SFT case. It is unclear exactly how preference pairs are represented as demonstrations and scored.

The principal evaluation metric is GPT-4o judgment of which response is closer to a single dataset reference, explicitly including length and style. This measures reference imitation rather than general response quality or alignment and can reward superficial matching. PPL and BERTScore have essentially the same limitation. Only GSM8K provides a clear task-level metric.

Most main experiments use only one training run. Repeated training is provided for two SFT configurations on one dataset, but not for DPO, SimPO, GSM8K, or the ablations. Several claimed improvements over RHO-Loss, LESS, and GREATS are near 50% and unsupported by uncertainty estimates.

The main experiments include the nominal holdout examples in training, weakening the holdout interpretation and potentially amplifying target-domain/style leakage. Strict separation is tested only for Yahoo SFT, where ICA is slightly worse than RHO-Loss. Strict-holdout evaluations are missing for the other datasets and alignment objectives.

Important simple controls are absent, particularly weighting by embedding similarity to the holdout set, response length, model loss, or known dataset quality scores. Figure 1 and the response-length analysis suggest that domain and length matching may explain substantial performance, but the experiments do not isolate the contribution of in-context loss scoring from these simpler signals.

The default method computes scores only once before training (R=1), contradicting repeated descriptions of dynamically reweighting examples as the model evolves. More frequent updates are evaluated only in a small, single-setting ablation.

The reweighting specification is incomplete: min-max normalization is undefined when batch scores are equal, and it is unclear over what effective batch weights are normalized given per-device batch size one and gradient accumulation. Scaling unnormalized weighted gradients also changes the effective update magnitude, which is not controlled against baselines.

The reported 1.5% overhead is based on one hardware/model/dataset configuration and excludes or insufficiently explains important costs such as contextual sequence expansion, storage, retrieval, and distributed score handling. This is insufficient to support a general minimal-overhead claim.

Overall, the idea is promising and the empirical breadth is notable, but the unverified core approximation, weak reference-matching evaluation, incomplete controls, and technical/reproducibility gaps prevent the work from meeting a top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and useful idea: approximate a candidate example’s effect on holdout loss through in-context demonstrations, avoiding the separately trained reference model required by RHO-Loss.

The empirical study is unusually broad, covering SFT, DPO, and SimPO; full-parameter and LoRA tuning; multiple 3B–8B LLaMA and Qwen backbones; quality, domain, and synthetic-noise settings; and several selection baselines.

Results against standard training are consistently strong, while performance is generally competitive with RHO-Loss at substantially lower reported overhead. The GSM8K corruption experiment provides particularly concrete evidence that the method can suppress harmful examples.
The paper includes useful ablations of demonstration count, update frequency, filtering versus reweighting, and embedding model, as well as runtime measurements and limited multi-seed experiments.
The presentation is clear, the algorithm is simple to integrate into existing training pipelines, and the dependence on a curated holdout set and limitations for on-policy learning are acknowledged.
weaknesses: The central in-context approximation is assumed rather than directly validated. The paper should measure how ICA scores correlate with the true change in holdout loss after training on candidates, or at least with the original holdout-loss/RHO scores across training. Without this, the claimed interpretation of ICA as approximating post-update holdout loss remains weakly supported even though the heuristic works empirically.

Most headline experiments use one training run and a GPT-4o judge. Multi-seed evidence covers only SFT on one dataset, while judge repetitions do not capture training variance. The judge protocol has no tie option, and response-order randomization or position-bias checks are not reported. Judge-independent metrics are provided only for Yahoo and GSM8K.

The default method computes scores only once at initialization (R=1), so descriptions of dynamically re-evaluating utility as parameters evolve overstate what is demonstrated in the main experiments. The update-frequency ablation is limited to one model and dataset and shows only small gains.

There are reproducibility inconsistencies. The paper names a seemingly nonexistent “LLaMA-3-3B-Instruct” model without exact model identifiers, and the Yahoo split arithmetic appears incorrect: 10,000 examples from each non-Sports category plus 3,000 Sports examples should not total 100,300 for the standard 10-category dataset. Code and prompts are promised but not included.

The evaluation mainly measures similarity to targets drawn from the same curated or domain-specific distribution, rather than broader instruction-following or alignment quality. This makes it difficult to determine whether ICA improves general capabilities or primarily encourages imitation of holdout-specific style and response length.

Preference-optimization comparisons omit several simple quality or confidence heuristics, while LESS and GREATS are evaluated only for SFT. In addition, the proposed min-max weighting is underspecified for equal-score batches and changes the aggregate gradient scale across batches, which may confound data valuation with effective learning-rate variation.
